content: 1. Develop, review, and implement a curriculum that integrates health and well-being into all subject areas. This includes creating content, pedagogical strategies, and associated resources such as assessment tools, sample lesson plans, and audiovisual materials. 2. Ensure that teacher training and professional development programs include health and well-being components. This should encompass pre-service teacher education, in-service professional learning, and the standards and certification processes for both graduate and in-service teachers. 3. Guarantee access to comprehensive school health services (SHS). These services should align with WHO guidelines and be delivered through formal agreements between schools (or local education departments) and health service providers. 4. Actively involve students in school governance. Include them on school councils, governance boards, and health-promoting school (HPS) design teams alongside parents, caregivers, and community members. Provide equal opportunities for all students to participate ethically and meaningfully in the governance, design, implementation, and evaluation of school health programs. 5. Engage parents, caregivers, and community members in school health initiatives. Include them on school councils, governance boards, and HPS design teams. Create opportunities for their meaningful participation in the governance, design, implementation, and evaluation of school health programs. 6. Establish systems to monitor and evaluate school health programs. Develop and share tools and practices for collecting, storing, and analyzing data at local, subnational, and national levels. Use this data to generate reports, disseminate findings, and adapt programs as needed. Invest in capacity-building activities for all stakeholders involved in the design, planning, implementation, and monitoring of HPS programs. 7. In France, school health is structured around four complementary components: education (life skills and disciplinary competencies), risk prevention (e.g., addressing addictive behaviors and sedentary lifestyles), protection, and service provision (e.g., consultations and health check-ups). All school staff, including school doctors, are expected to contribute to this health promotion dynamic. 8. French school doctors, who are attached to the Ministry of Education, undergo specialized training after graduating from medical school and passing a public service competition. This training, provided by the School of Public Health in coordination with the Ministry of Education, includes an individualized program lasting 8–16 weeks, followed by autonomous work in schools under the supervision of experienced mentors. 9. The training of French school doctors has been revised over the past 15 years to align with 10 core competencies specific to their role. These competencies include coordinating actions, managing risks, evaluating systems, advising on student health, training school staff, communicating data, promoting safe school environments, exercising medical expertise, co-designing health projects, and using scientific data on child and adolescent health. 10. Government-led social transfer programs have significant positive impacts on adolescents, including improved school attendance, food security, and mental health outcomes. These programs can also delay early marriage, reduce unpaid labor, and decrease risky sexual behaviors. 11. To enhance social protection for adolescents, governments should expand coverage to include older adolescents, improve program responsiveness to adolescent needs, and strengthen linkages between social protection and health services. Conditional and unconditional cash transfer programs should incentivize health-promoting behaviors such as school attendance, medical check-ups, and vaccinations. 12. Multisectoral interventions, such as those implemented in Kenya’s Adolescent Girls Initiative, demonstrate the effectiveness of combining community-based programs with education, health, and wealth-creation interventions. These approaches can reduce early pregnancy rates and improve long-term health and economic outcomes for adolescent girls in impoverished settings. 13. Criminal justice systems must adopt child-friendly and gender-sensitive approaches to protect the rights and well-being of children. This includes establishing specialized units within the police, judiciary, and court systems, as well as providing legal and psychological support for children in conflict with the law. 14. Preventive programs should address the root causes of juvenile offenses, such as poverty and family violence, and decriminalize minor offenses like truancy and begging. Early interventions should focus on children below the minimum age of criminal responsibility, offering multidisciplinary support to address behavioral issues. 15. Countries should establish a minimum age of criminal responsibility that reflects the evolving nature of adolescent maturity. This age should be set at no lower than 14 years, with no exceptions for serious offenses. If a child’s age cannot be verified, they should be given the benefit of the doubt and not held criminally responsible. 16. Comprehensive child justice systems should apply to all individuals under 18 years of age at the time of the offense. These systems should include specialized services such as probation, counseling, and legal assistance to ensure the best interests of the child are upheld.
